title: Fish Physiology
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 300L Fish Physiology curriculum: respiration and gas exchange across gills, circulatory system, osmoregulation in freshwater versus marine fish, digestive and nutritional physiology, endocrine control of growth and reproduction, nervous and sensory systems, excretion, thermal biology (poikilothermy), and buoyancy control. Kept distinct from Fish Pathology & Parasitology (FIS303) by focusing on normal function rather than disease.

questions.question: The primary site of gas exchange in bony fish is the:
questions.correct_answer: Gill lamellae
questions.explanation: The thin, highly vascularized gill lamellae provide the large surface area needed for oxygen uptake and carbon dioxide release from the blood.

questions.question: The countercurrent flow of water and blood across the fish gill is important because it:
options: Maximizes the concentration gradient for oxygen diffusion along the whole length of the lamella
Prevents the gills from drying out
Slows down the rate of oxygen uptake to conserve energy
questions.correct_answer: Maximizes the concentration gradient for oxygen diffusion along the whole length of the lamella
questions.explanation: Because water flows opposite to blood flow, a diffusion gradient favoring oxygen movement into the blood is maintained along the entire gill lamella, greatly increasing extraction efficiency.

questions.question: Which structure in fish gills supports accessory air-breathing in species like Clarias gariepinus?
questions.correct_answer: Suprabranchial (arborescent) organ
questions.explanation: Clarias and related catfish possess arborescent (tree-like) suprabranchial organs that allow them to breathe atmospheric air, enabling survival in poorly oxygenated water.

questions.question: The heart of a typical teleost fish is best described as:
options: A two-chambered pump with a single atrium and single ventricle carrying deoxygenated blood
A four-chambered pump similar to mammals
A three-chambered pump with two atria and one ventricle
A structure with no distinct chambers
questions.correct_answer: A two-chambered pump with a single atrium and single ventricle carrying deoxygenated blood
questions.explanation: Fish have a single circulatory loop; the heart pumps deoxygenated blood to the gills where it is oxygenated before going to the body, so the heart itself only handles deoxygenated blood.

questions.question: In fish circulation, blood flows in the sequence:
options: Sinus venosus to atrium to ventricle to bulbus/conus arteriosus to gills to body
Ventricle to atrium to sinus venosus to gills to body
Gills to atrium to ventricle to body to sinus venosus
Atrium to gills to ventricle to body
questions.correct_answer: Sinus venosus to atrium to ventricle to bulbus/conus arteriosus to gills to body
questions.explanation: Venous blood collects in the sinus venosus, passes to the atrium, then the ventricle, is pushed out through the bulbus (or conus) arteriosus to the gills for oxygenation, and then to the body.

questions.question: Osmoregulation in a freshwater teleost fish primarily involves:
options: Actively absorbing salts through the gills and excreting large volumes of dilute urine
Actively excreting salts through the gills and producing small volumes of concentrated urine
Drinking large amounts of surrounding water
Having no need to regulate internal salt or water balance
questions.correct_answer: Actively absorbing salts through the gills and excreting large volumes of dilute urine
questions.explanation: Freshwater fish live in a hypotonic environment, so water constantly enters by osmosis; they excrete large volumes of dilute urine and actively take up ions via chloride cells in the gills.

questions.question: Marine teleost fish, in contrast to freshwater teleosts, maintain water balance by:
options: Drinking seawater and actively excreting excess salt through the gills
Refusing to drink water at all
Absorbing salt through the skin only
Producing large volumes of dilute urine
questions.correct_answer: Drinking seawater and actively excreting excess salt through the gills
questions.explanation: Marine fish live in a hypertonic environment and lose water by osmosis, so they drink seawater and use chloride cells in the gills to actively pump out the excess salt taken in.

questions.question: Chloride cells, key to osmoregulation in teleosts, are mainly located in the:
questions.correct_answer: Gill epithelium
questions.explanation: Chloride (ionocyte) cells embedded in the gill epithelium actively transport ions and are the principal site of osmoregulatory ion exchange in teleost fish.

questions.question: The main nitrogenous waste excreted by most freshwater teleost fish is:
questions.correct_answer: Ammonia
questions.explanation: Most teleost fish are ammonotelic, excreting the majority of nitrogenous waste as ammonia directly across the gills, which is efficient because they are surrounded by abundant water to dilute it.

questions.question: The kidney in bony fish contributes to osmoregulation mainly by:
options: Filtering blood and adjusting urine volume and composition
questions.correct_answer: Filtering blood and adjusting urine volume and composition
questions.explanation: The fish kidney filters blood through nephrons and regulates the volume and ionic composition of urine, complementing the gills in maintaining osmotic balance.

questions.question: The stomach of carnivorous fish typically differs from that of herbivorous fish by being:
options: More muscular and acidic, adapted for protein digestion
Longer and coiled for fermentation of plant material
Lined with keratinized plates for grinding algae
questions.correct_answer: More muscular and acidic, adapted for protein digestion
questions.explanation: Carnivorous fish generally have a true, acid-secreting stomach suited to breaking down animal protein, while many herbivores lack a true stomach and rely on a long gut instead.

questions.question: Pyloric caeca, found in many teleost fish, function primarily to:
options: Increase the surface area for digestion and absorption of nutrients
questions.correct_answer: Increase the surface area for digestion and absorption of nutrients
questions.explanation: Pyloric caeca are finger-like outpocketings near the junction of the stomach and intestine that increase the absorptive and enzymatic surface area of the gut.

questions.question: In fish digestion, the enzyme trypsin is secreted mainly by the:
questions.correct_answer: Pancreas
questions.explanation: The pancreas (often diffuse tissue in teleosts) secretes trypsin and other proteolytic enzymes into the intestine to digest dietary protein.

questions.question: Fish that lack a true stomach and rely on continuous feeding with a long intestine, such as many cyprinids, are typically:
questions.correct_answer: Herbivorous or detritivorous species
questions.explanation: Agastric (stomachless) fish are commonly herbivores or detritivores whose diet requires prolonged, gradual digestion rather than acid-based protein breakdown.

questions.question: The swim bladder in physoclistous fish regulates buoyancy by:
options: Exchanging gas with the blood via the gas gland and rete mirabile, with no direct connection to the gut
Gulping air directly from the water surface through a duct to the gut
questions.correct_answer: Exchanging gas with the blood via the gas gland and rete mirabile, with no direct connection to the gut
questions.explanation: Physoclistous fish lack a pneumatic duct; gas is secreted into or resorbed from the swim bladder through specialized gas glands and the countercurrent rete mirabile.

questions.question: Physostomous fish, unlike physoclistous fish, regulate the gas in their swim bladder by:
options: Gulping air at the surface through a pneumatic duct connecting the bladder to the gut
Secreting gas solely via the gas gland
Having no swim bladder at all
Absorbing dissolved oxygen through the skin
questions.correct_answer: Gulping air at the surface through a pneumatic duct connecting the bladder to the gut
questions.explanation: Physostomous fish (e.g., many primitive teleosts) retain a pneumatic duct linking the swim bladder to the esophagus, allowing them to fill or release gas by gulping air.

questions.question: Fish are described as poikilothermic (ectothermic) because they:
options: Have a body temperature that fluctuates with the surrounding water temperature
Generate metabolic heat to maintain a constant body temperature
Cannot survive temperature changes at all
Regulate temperature using the swim bladder
questions.correct_answer: Have a body temperature that fluctuates with the surrounding water temperature
questions.explanation: Most fish are ectotherms whose body temperature closely tracks ambient water temperature because they generate little metabolic heat and lose it rapidly to water.

questions.question: An increase in water temperature within a fish's tolerable range generally causes its metabolic rate to:
questions.correct_answer: Increase
questions.explanation: As ectotherms, fish metabolic rate rises with temperature (within tolerance limits) because biochemical reaction rates increase, raising oxygen demand.

questions.question: The pituitary gland in fish is often called the 'master gland' because it:
options: Releases hormones that regulate the activity of other endocrine glands
Produces all the fish's digestive enzymes
questions.correct_answer: Releases hormones that regulate the activity of other endocrine glands
questions.explanation: The pituitary secretes hormones such as gonadotropins and growth hormone that regulate the thyroid, gonads, and other target tissues, coordinating growth, reproduction, and osmoregulation.

questions.question: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) and gonadotropins are central to induced spawning in fish because they:
options: Stimulate final gonadal maturation, ovulation, and spawning
Regulate only the fish's swimming speed
questions.correct_answer: Stimulate final gonadal maturation, ovulation, and spawning
questions.explanation: GnRH stimulates pituitary release of gonadotropins, which act on the gonads to trigger final oocyte maturation and ovulation, the physiological basis of hormone-induced spawning.

questions.question: The thyroid gland in fish primarily produces hormones that regulate:
questions.correct_answer: Growth, development, and metabolism
questions.explanation: Thyroid hormones (thyroxine and triiodothyronine) influence growth, metabolic rate, and developmental processes such as smoltification in salmonids.

questions.question: Cortisol released from the interrenal tissue in fish under stress functions mainly to:
options: Mobilize energy reserves and help the fish cope with the stressor
questions.correct_answer: Mobilize energy reserves and help the fish cope with the stressor
questions.explanation: Cortisol is the primary stress hormone in fish, promoting gluconeogenesis and energy mobilization as part of the physiological stress response, though chronic elevation can suppress growth and immunity.

questions.question: Chronic stress in cultured fish, marked by prolonged cortisol elevation, most commonly results in:
options: Suppressed growth and increased susceptibility to disease
Immediate death within minutes in all cases
questions.correct_answer: Suppressed growth and increased susceptibility to disease
questions.explanation: Prolonged cortisol elevation diverts energy from growth and reproduction and suppresses immune responses, making chronically stressed fish more vulnerable to disease.

questions.question: The lateral line system in fish primarily functions to detect:
options: Water movement, vibration, and pressure changes in the surrounding environment
questions.correct_answer: Water movement, vibration, and pressure changes in the surrounding environment
questions.explanation: Neuromasts along the lateral line detect hydrodynamic disturbances, helping fish sense currents, obstacles, predators, and prey even in darkness.

questions.question: Olfactory (smell) receptors in fish are primarily used for detecting:
options: Chemical cues in water such as food odors, pheromones, and alarm substances
questions.correct_answer: Chemical cues in water such as food odors, pheromones, and alarm substances
questions.explanation: Olfactory organs in fish detect waterborne chemical signals important for locating food, recognizing mates, and responding to alarm substances released by injured conspecifics.

questions.question: The cerebellum in the fish brain is primarily responsible for:
questions.correct_answer: Coordination of movement and balance
questions.explanation: The cerebellum integrates sensory input to coordinate muscular movement and maintain balance, and is often well developed in active swimming species.

questions.question: Red (slow-twitch) muscle fibers in fish are primarily used for:
options: Sustained, aerobic swimming such as cruising
Brief bursts of high-speed escape swimming
questions.correct_answer: Sustained, aerobic swimming such as cruising
questions.explanation: Red muscle is highly vascularized, rich in mitochondria and myoglobin, and fueled aerobically, making it suited to prolonged, sustained swimming rather than short bursts.

questions.question: White (fast-twitch) muscle fibers in fish are adapted for:
options: Rapid, powerful, short-duration bursts of anaerobic swimming
Continuous slow cruising over long distances
questions.correct_answer: Rapid, powerful, short-duration bursts of anaerobic swimming
questions.explanation: White muscle relies mainly on anaerobic glycolysis and fatigues quickly, making it suited to sudden bursts of speed such as escape responses or prey capture.

questions.question: Vitellogenesis, the process central to oocyte development in female fish, refers to:
options: The deposition of yolk protein into developing oocytes under hormonal control
The fertilization of eggs by sperm
The hatching of eggs into larvae
The absorption of the yolk sac after hatching
questions.correct_answer: The deposition of yolk protein into developing oocytes under hormonal control
questions.explanation: Vitellogenesis is the estrogen-driven synthesis of vitellogenin by the liver and its uptake into oocytes as yolk, providing nutrient reserves for the developing embryo.

questions.question: In most male teleost fish, sperm are produced and matured within the:
questions.correct_answer: Testes
questions.explanation: The testes contain seminiferous tubules or lobules where spermatogenesis occurs, producing mature spermatozoa for fertilization.

questions.question: Gonadosomatic index (GSI), commonly used to assess fish reproductive condition, is calculated as:
options: Gonad weight divided by total body weight, multiplied by 100
Total body weight divided by gonad weight
Length of the fish divided by gonad weight
Number of eggs divided by body length
questions.correct_answer: Gonad weight divided by total body weight, multiplied by 100
questions.explanation: GSI expresses gonad weight as a percentage of total body weight and is widely used to track gonadal development and spawning readiness.

questions.question: Fish blood typically contains hemoglobin dissolved within:
questions.correct_answer: Red blood cells (erythrocytes)
questions.explanation: As in most vertebrates, fish hemoglobin is packaged within nucleated red blood cells, which transport oxygen from the gills to the tissues.

questions.question: A rise in environmental carbon dioxide and a corresponding drop in water pH can impair fish respiration mainly by:
options: Reducing the oxygen-carrying capacity and affinity of hemoglobin (Bohr/Root effect)
Directly destroying the gill filaments within seconds
Having no physiological effect on fish
questions.correct_answer: Reducing the oxygen-carrying capacity and affinity of hemoglobin (Bohr/Root effect)
questions.explanation: Elevated CO2 lowers blood pH, which via the Bohr and Root effects reduces hemoglobin's affinity for and capacity to carry oxygen, impairing gas transport.

questions.question: The liver in fish plays a central physiological role by:
options: Storing glycogen and lipid reserves and synthesizing key plasma proteins including vitellogenin
Regulating swim bladder gas volume directly
questions.correct_answer: Storing glycogen and lipid reserves and synthesizing key plasma proteins including vitellogenin
questions.explanation: The fish liver is a major metabolic organ for energy storage, detoxification, and the hormonally-driven synthesis of proteins such as vitellogenin during reproduction.

questions.question: Fish exposed to low dissolved oxygen (hypoxia) commonly respond physiologically by:
options: Increasing ventilation (opercular beat) rate and, in some species, using accessory air-breathing organs
Producing more melanin in the skin
questions.correct_answer: Increasing ventilation (opercular beat) rate and, in some species, using accessory air-breathing organs
questions.explanation: Under hypoxic stress, fish typically increase gill ventilation to extract more oxygen, and air-breathing species may surface more frequently to gulp atmospheric air.

questions.question: In fish osmoregulation, the process by which chloride cells actively excrete excess sodium and chloride ions in marine species is driven mainly by the enzyme:
questions.correct_answer: Na+/K+-ATPase
questions.explanation: Na+/K+-ATPase in the basolateral membrane of chloride cells powers the active ion transport that allows marine fish to excrete excess salt against a concentration gradient.

questions.question: Euryhaline fish, such as tilapia, are notable physiologically for their ability to:
options: Tolerate and osmoregulate across a wide range of environmental salinities
Survive only in a very narrow, fixed salinity range
Live exclusively in deep marine waters
questions.correct_answer: Tolerate and osmoregulate across a wide range of environmental salinities
questions.explanation: Euryhaline species possess flexible osmoregulatory mechanisms that let them move between freshwater, brackish, and marine environments, unlike stenohaline species restricted to a narrow salinity range.

questions.question: Growth hormone (somatotropin) in fish, released from the pituitary, primarily promotes:
questions.correct_answer: Somatic (body) growth and protein synthesis
questions.explanation: Growth hormone stimulates protein synthesis and tissue growth, often mediated by insulin-like growth factors, and is a key target in selective breeding and growth-enhancement studies.
